newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks shaky on certification but fight Dow.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks shaky on certification but fight Dow.

text.p: Mexican stocks closed weaker on Thursday after the U.S. Congress took a step toward decertifying Mexico as a drug-fighting ally.

The leading IPC share index ended down 12.70 points, or 0.34 percent, at 3,745.39. On the broad market, 101 stocks changed hands in total, of which losers outpaced gainers by 47 to 35. Trading volume was restrained at 83.8 million shares.
Nonetheless, traders and analysts noted the market managed to fend off a very sharp drop on Wall Street.
"What, with the Dow and the decertification, the bourse has done darned well. It didn't drop because there are no stocks, no one wants to sell at these levels," a floor trader said.

The Dow index fell 160.48 points to close at 6,878.89 --the fifth steepest fall in point terms in the history of the average. on fears the Federal Reserve's policy-making committee might raise U.S. interest rates at its meeting on March 25.

"What needs to be stressed is that the bourse withstood the fall on Wall Street very well. They (moved to) decertify us, but we have three months grace in which the market will be calmer," said Gerardo Copca, an equity analyst with the Finamex brokerage in Mexico City.
"The FOMC meeting is what is weighing most heavily, and I believe the market is moving wisely," he said.
"A hike in U.S. base rates would hurt us more (than decertification) because foreign capital would flow towards the U.S. bond market," Copca added.
In late trade, the U.S. House of Representatives voted to overturn President Bill Clinton's finding that Mexico is an ally in the war on drugs. The vote was 228 to 195.

Nonetheless, the legislators took the sting out of the move by agreeing to waive economic sanctions and give Clinton 90 days' grace to garner "reliable assurances of substantial progress" in Mexico's drug war efforts.
Traders said the House vote to censure Mexico's anti-drug fight did not come as a body blow to the market as had been expected.

"Most dealers bore in mind they were not going to certify us, and that Clinton will likely apply a veto, with some ripples along the way, so nothing happened. The market had discounted the move since yesterday," the floor trader added.

"Just relax and take it easy, it won't be that bad," another floor trader said, noting that tension on the trading floor eased considerably after the IPC bottomed out at 3,272.35 points in early trade.
"Dealers saw the market in a good light once it respected strong support at 3,730 points. ... There are real buyers, I don't think it was mere window dressing," the trader added.

Telecommunications company Telmex L shares weighed most heavily on the market, accounting for 14 percent of all shares traded during the session and ended down 8 centavos (1 cent) at 15.80 pesos ($1.97).
Telmex fell in tandem with its American Depositary Receipts, off 1/8 to 39-3/8, but the latter slid to far less an extent than Dow index, traders noted.

Financial group GFB B shares ended up 10 centavos (1 cent) to 2.94 pesos (37 cents), after staging a recovery from an early low of 2.80 pesos (35 cents). Traders said the stock recovered on bargain hunting and technical factors.
